lesson.title: What Happens When Atoms Gain or Lose Electrons
lesson.summary: Writing the electron configuration of an ion starts from the neutral atom's configuration and adds electrons to form anions or removes them to form cations, with transition metals following the special rule of losing s electrons before d electrons.
lesson.body:
An ion is just an atom, or a group of atoms, that has gained or lost electrons and therefore carries a net charge. Writing an ion's electron configuration starts from exactly the same neutral atom configuration you already know how to build; you simply add or remove the right number of electrons and then figure out which subshell those electrons come from or go to. For anions, negatively charged ions formed by gaining electrons, the new electrons simply continue filling subshells in the usual Aufbau order, right where the neutral atom's configuration left off.

Chlorine again offers a clean example, this time as an anion. Neutral chlorine is [Ne] 3s2 3p5, with 17 electrons. The chloride ion, Cl minus, forms when chlorine gains one electron, giving 18 electrons total. That extra electron completes the 3p subshell, which can hold up to 6, so chloride's configuration is [Ne] 3s2 3p6, identical in electron count and arrangement to argon (also 18 electrons, [Ne] 3s2 3p6, or written in full, 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6). Chloride and argon are described as isoelectronic, meaning they have the exact same number of electrons arranged in exactly the same configuration, even though they are different elements with different numbers of protons.

Cations, positively charged ions formed by losing electrons, work the same way in reverse for main group elements: remove electrons from the highest n, outermost subshell first. Sodium, [Ne] 3s1, loses its single 3s electron to form Na plus, giving [Ne], which is isoelectronic with neutral neon. Magnesium, [Ne] 3s2, loses both 3s electrons to form Mg2 plus, also reaching [Ne].

Transition metals introduce one genuine wrinkle that trips up a lot of students, and it is worth being precise about it. When a transition metal forms a cation, electrons are removed from the s subshell before the d subshell, even though, during Aufbau filling of the neutral atom, that same s subshell filled before the d subshell. Iron's neutral configuration, worked out earlier as [Ar] 4s2 3d6, loses electrons from 4s first when it ionizes: Fe2 plus is [Ar] 3d6, not [Ar] 4s2 3d4. Losing a third electron to form Fe3 plus then removes one electron from 3d, giving [Ar] 3d5, a configuration that is especially stable because the d subshell is now exactly half filled, the same extra stability that made chromium an Aufbau exception in its neutral state. This s before d removal order happens because once electrons occupy the 3d subshell, they raise the energy of the remaining 4s electrons more than 3d, effectively reversing which subshell is easiest to strip an electron from.

The core lesson is that ion configurations are not a new set of rules, only a modified starting point and, for transition metals, a modified removal order. Get the neutral atom's configuration right using Aufbau, Pauli, and Hund's rule, know whether the ion is gaining or losing electrons, and, for transition metals specifically, remember that s empties before d. Everything else follows directly from the same subshell logic you have already been using throughout this entire unit.
